note: Quotes written by ear and passed line-by-line editorial review. Everything else in the corpus is superseded machine-optimised backfill and is not published.
quotes: Say no to a hundred good things. That's the only way the great thing gets your whole attention.
You don't find focus. You make it, by throwing out everything that isn't the one thing.
Every yes is a promise to defend something for years. Most of them aren't worth the argument.
Focus costs you things you like. If it doesn't hurt a bit, you haven't focused.
Every feature we took out made it better. That should tell you something.
The best thing on your list gets ruined by the third best thing on your list.
You cut far more than you keep. That isn't restraint, that's the work.
Half the things we were proudest of never left the building. That isn't waste, that's taste.
You'll know your standards are real the first time you throw out something good.
The stuff you don't ship is doing work too. It's keeping the rest of it clean.
Killing good work feels like losing. It's the only way anything great gets out the door.
If nobody's upset about what you cut, you didn't cut enough.
The argument you keep avoiding is the thing you should have killed months ago.
Taste is knowing which good idea to throw away.
You don't get to great by adding. You get there by having the nerve to take things out.
The easiest trap is keeping something alive just because you've spent six months on it.
The hardest thing to cut is the part you thought of.
You'll miss it for about a week. Then you'll wonder why it took you so long.
Some things work fine and still have to go. That's the part almost nobody can do.
Everything you cut is time the rest of it gets.
A long list is what you make instead of a decision.
What you've already spent isn't a reason. It's just why it hurts.
Half of what you're doing is there because nobody ever stopped it.
Complicated is what you ship when you run out of time to think.
Anybody can make it complicated. That's the default. Getting it simple is the work.
People confuse simple with easy. Simple is what's left after the hard part is done.
If it's still complicated, you didn't finish. You stopped.
Most people can't make things simple because they can't stand being wrong that many times.
Complexity is a great place to hide. It lets people pretend they know what they're doing when they're actually just lost.
Getting it simple takes longer and looks like less. That's why hardly anyone does it.
You have to understand the whole thing before you can cut it down. Most people quit at good enough.
Simple isn't a style you pick. It's what's left when you refuse to stop thinking.
You're going to die. That one fact deletes more bad decisions than a year of thinking.
Nothing clears a calendar like remembering how it ends.
The ground doesn't care what people thought of you. That's the most useful thing about it.
Fear of looking stupid dies the second you remember you're on a clock.
Most of what you're protecting won't outlive you. Spend it now.
The end is the only boundary that makes people honest about what they actually care about.
You can't take your reputation with you. Stop managing it and go do the work.
Ask what you'd drop if you had a year left. Then drop it today, because you might.
Pride is heavy, and you're carrying it toward a hole in the ground.
The end doesn't make life sad. It makes the choices simple.
Nobody's going to open it up and check. You'll know. That's the entire reason.
The parts a customer never sees are the ones that tell you whether anyone cared.
You can feel when the inside was done properly. You just can't point at why.
If you'd be embarrassed to show someone the inside, you're not finished.
Quality is what you do after the review is over and nobody's watching.
The work nobody inspects is where your standards actually live.
People can't see the care. They can feel it, and they just know they like it.
You're not doing it so they notice. You're doing it so you can sleep.
Cutting a corner nobody sees still cuts the corner.
Two things can look identical and only one of them was made by someone who cared.
Committees don't make things. They make things safe, which is the same as making them dull.
Ask a hundred people what they want and you'll get a list of what already exists.
A customer can tell you what's broken. They can't tell you what's missing.
Consensus is just the average of everyone's fear.
Everyone in the room agreeing is a warning, not a result.
Taste isn't democratic. Somebody has to have the stomach to look at the room and say no.
The numbers tell you what happened. They've got nothing to say about what to do next.
A group will never approve the thing that scares it. That's usually the thing.
If you need a study to tell you it's good, it isn't.
You'll be the only one who can see it for a while. That isn't evidence you're wrong.
The room will have data and you'll have a feeling. Sometimes the feeling wins, and you have to live with that.
Everyone agrees with you afterwards. That's not the same as help.
Trusting your gut is cheap until your name is on it.
You don't get the proof first. You get it after you've spent the money.
The hard part isn't knowing. It's being the only one who knows and going anyway.
Nobody thanks you for the risk while it's still a risk.
You can be talked out of anything you haven't decided to defend.
One person who cares will outwork ten who are merely qualified.
A CV tells you where somebody has been. It says nothing about whether they'll fight for it.
Every mediocre hire costs you two great ones. They take the seat and they lower the bar.
You can't teach someone to care. You can only find the ones who already do.
A big team is what you build when you don't know which five people matter.
If somebody needs to be told what excellent looks like, they aren't it.
The people worth having don't need to be managed. They just need everyone else to get out of their way so they can build something.
Hire someone better than you and the job stops being management. It becomes getting out of the way.
Talent is common. Finding people who won't settle is the hard part.
Somebody has to go first, and going first means being wrong in public for a while.
You're not giving people what they asked for. You're taking responsibility for what they'll want.
The first reaction to anything genuinely new is discomfort. Sit with it instead of sanding it off.
If everyone likes it immediately, you built what they already had.
Showing people something they didn't ask for is the whole job. It's also why it's lonely.
You can follow the audience or you can lead it. You can't do both in the same product.
People will tell you it's obvious about a year after they told you it was mad.
You have to decide what people deserve before they know it exists. Nobody votes on that.
Watching it fall apart is unbearable for a month, but it's useful for a decade.
Expertise is mostly a list of things you've quietly stopped questioning.
The day you stop being the authority is the day you can try something again.
Starting over is only humiliating if you were pretending to be finished.
Being the expert costs more than it pays. You spend the whole time defending the last idea.
Nothing frees you up like having nothing left to protect.
You learn more in the year after a project collapses than in the five years you spent making it work.
Success makes you careful, and careful is the slowest way to work.
Process exists so people who can't tell good from bad can still have an opinion.
Every layer of approval is somebody protecting themselves at the product's expense.
Big companies don't die of bad ideas. They die of the procedures built to prevent them.
When the process matters more than the thing, it's already over.
A system should make good work easy. Most of them just make bad work survivable.
Ask who a rule protects. It's almost never the person using what you made.
A big company will take someone's raw conviction and turn it into paperwork within a week if you let them.
You can't schedule taste. You hire it and then you leave it alone.
Anybody can follow a checklist. That's why no checklist ever made anything great.
There's a happiness in getting one small thing exactly right that nothing else touches.
You should be slightly embarrassed by how much you care. That's how you know it's yours.
Somebody made the thing you love. They sat there and got it right for you, and you'll never meet them.
The best work is a gift to people you'll never know. It's just what it is.
When it's finally right you feel it before you can explain it, and explaining it takes years.
Make something so good that people feel looked after when they use it.
Falling in love with an object sounds ridiculous until you've made one worth loving.
Everything great you've ever used was somebody's obsession. Nobody built it because it was reasonable.
The point isn't that they remember who you were. It's that you put something beautiful into the world that wasn't there before.
Working with people who are better than you on something that matters is as good as it gets.
The moment it finally works is worth every miserable week that came before it.
Nothing beats a room full of people who all refuse to ship something ordinary.
Life is too short to make things you'd be ashamed to sign.
You'll remember three or four projects. Make sure you actually chose them.
Being paid well to make junk is still a bad deal. You only get the one life.
The best years are the ones where you were slightly out of your depth with people you admired.
You can spend your life making money, or you can spend it making things people keep. Pick one.
You look at six months of somebody's work and say start over. Then you drive home wondering if you're just cruel.
Telling people who tried hard that it isn't good enough is the worst part of the job. You do it anyway.
Everyone wants the standard. Almost nobody wants to be the one enforcing it at six on a Friday.
You'll be called difficult by people who were quietly relieved somebody made them do it properly.
The hardest thing to say is not yet, and you have to say it to people you like.
Holding a line when everyone else is exhausted is incredibly lonely. They just want to go home, and you're the one holding the door closed.
It costs something to be the only one who won't settle, and mostly what it costs is company.
The tiring part isn't the standard. It's being the only one who sees what's wrong with it.
Once in a while you want somebody else to spot it first, so you don't have to be the one.
You get tired of being the reason everyone's evening got longer.
There's a particular exhaustion in noticing. You can't switch it off and nobody asked you to start.
Every time you stop the room you spend a little of whatever people feel about you.
You'd love to let it go. That's the part nobody believes about you.
Some days you hope nobody points at the flaw, because then you'd have to say something.
The worst version of this is being right and wishing you weren't.
You stop being able to unsee things. That's the real exhaustion.
